title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction: Setting (from §§XXXV-XXXVI): the configuration of a moving, perfectly flexible thread is described by the tangent angle φ(s,t). Arclength s is a material (Lagrangian) label, and t is time. Then x_s = sin φ and y_s = cos φ. The mass of the element ds is Σ(s) ds. On this page Euler finishes the kinematics. In order to perform the assumed motion, the element must be acted on by the 'required' forces (Σ ds/2g) x_tt along AX and (Σ ds/2g) y_tt along XM. The factor 1/2g comes from his usual unit convention: g is the height fallen in one second, so a force equals mass times acceleration divided by 2g. §XXXVII is a verbal statement of d'Alembert's principle. Euler distinguishes the 'vires ad motum producendum immediate requisitae' from the forces actually acting. The two systems must be equivalent. Therefore, if the required forces are applied in reverse, they balance the actual forces, and at that instant the thread is in equilibrium. This reduces the dynamics of the thread to the statics already worked out earlier in the paper. §XXXVIII begins the step: to the given forces p ds (tangential) and q ds (normal), add the reversed inertial forces along XA and MX. The text then resolves these along the tangent MT and the normal mr. The next page gives the effective loads p ds + (Σ ds/2g)(x_tt sin φ + y_tt cos φ) and q ds + (Σ ds/2g)(y_tt sin φ − x_tt cos φ). These are substituted into the static equilibrium equations of the thread, giving the PDE system of §XL (four equations). The problem served is deriving the equations of motion of a flexible string (or chain) under arbitrary loads, as a lead-in to the elastic case.
errors: In §XXXVIII the printed text says 'primo vim in directione XA = (Σds/2g)(ddy/dt²)' and no 'secundo' clause follows. Consistency with the preceding lines and with the next page requires two clauses. First, a force along XA equal to (Σds/2g)(ddx/dt²). Second, a force along MX equal to (Σds/2g)(ddy/dt²). A line or clause appears to have been dropped in typesetting, merging the two clauses. This is a typographical omission; the subsequent resolution on p.409 is correct.
The signs of the reversed inertial forces on p.409 depend on the orientation conventions for p, q, XA and MX. They are internally consistent with Euler's earlier conventions; no substantive error.

ideas.what: Required (inertial) forces m·a/(2g) for an element of a continuum, in fixed Cartesian directions, with partial derivatives at fixed material label s
ideas.modern_name: Lagrangian description; Newton's second law for a continuum element (Euler's units convention)
ideas.where_published: E177 'Découverte d'un nouveau principe de mécanique'; many other Euler papers

ideas.what: Reduction of the motion problem to an equilibrium problem by applying reversed required forces
ideas.where_published: Used by Euler in several works on flexible and elastic bodies; discussed by Truesdell (1960) in his account of the rational mechanics of flexible or elastic bodies

ideas.what: Resolution of the inertial forces into tangential and normal components, to be inserted into the static string equations
ideas.modern_name: Intrinsic (tangent-normal) form of the string equations of motion
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler / Jacob Bernoulli tradition for static catenary equations
ideas.where_published: E410 itself; Truesdell's commentary in Opera omnia ser. II vols. 10-11

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, well-documented application of d'Alembert's principle to the flexible thread. E410 is covered in Truesdell's history. The only oddity is a typographical omission in §XXXVIII.
transcription_corrections: The transcription faithfully reproduces the printed 'XA = (Σds/2g)(ddy/dt²)'. The intended text is evidently 'XA = (Σds/2g)(ddx/dt²), secundo vim in directione MX = (Σds/2g)(ddy/dt²)'; the omission is in the original print.
